q: What is the passage mainly about?
o: Why mercury is more useful than water for building pumps
How weather offices first learned to forecast storms
Why early scholars refused to accept the results of experiments
How a puzzle about pumps led to the discovery that air has weight
x: The passage follows the pump-makers' "awkward fact" to the mercury tube and the idea that water is "pushed up by the weight of the air". Weather is not mentioned at all; the tube is described only as "an instrument for measuring the air itself".

q: According to the passage, what had pump-makers noticed?
o: Their pumps worked better on mountains than in valleys
A suction pump could not raise water beyond a certain height
Water rose faster in narrow pipes than in wide ones
Their pumps lifted mercury more easily than water
x: The first paragraph says a suction pump "could not lift water more than about ten metres". The difference between mountains and valleys was noticed later, in the mercury column, not in pumps.

q: The passage suggests that on a mountain the air presses down:
o: more heavily than in a valley, so it holds up a taller column
less heavily than in a valley, so it holds up a shorter column
with the same force as in a valley, since air weighs the same everywhere
not at all, so the gap at the top of the tube disappears
x: The column balances "the same weight of air", and it "stood lower on a mountain than in a valley"; a shorter column means less weight of air pressing down. A heavier push would give a taller column, the opposite of what was seen.

q: As used in the first paragraph, the word "awkward" most nearly means:
o: clumsy in the way it moves
embarrassing to talk about in company
difficult to hold or carry
troublesome because it did not fit the accepted idea
x: The fact is "awkward" because a nature that rushes to fill any gap should lift water to any height, yet pumps stopped at a limit. "Clumsy" is the word's everyday meaning for people, not for a fact.

q: In the second paragraph, the phrase "just as the idea predicted" refers to the prediction that:
o: the mercury would fill the whole tube and leave no gap
a heavier liquid would need a shorter column than water
the column would rise and fall slightly from day to day
the gap at the top of the tube would slowly fill with air
x: The sentence explains the prediction itself: "a heavier liquid needs less height to balance the same weight of air", so the mercury column was "much shorter than ten metres". The daily rise and fall was noticed "soon" afterwards, not predicted.

q: Which title best fits the passage?
o: Why Meat Rots Faster in Open Jars
The Life Cycle of the Common Fly
How a Fair Comparison Overturned an Old Belief
How New Instruments Changed Early Science
x: The passage tells how the jar test disproved the belief that "rotting meat produced worms" and praises "its comparison". It is not about instruments: the method "does not depend on clever instruments".

q: Why did the experimenter cover some jars with fine cloth in his second test?
o: To keep the meat from rotting too quickly
To let flies reach the meat more easily
To stop mice from getting into the jars
To answer the objection that sealed jars had kept out air
x: Critics said sealing "had shut out the fresh air that life required", so the cloth "let air in but kept flies out". It did not help flies reach the meat; it kept them away from it.

q: The passage suggests that people who believed meat produced maggots went wrong mainly because they:
o: could not watch closely enough to see where the maggots came from
did not care about observing things carefully
had studied only meat and never looked at grain
refused to repeat any test that gave a surprising result
x: They "had no way of watching every fly that landed", and the experiment showed that flies lay eggs where they land. They were not careless: the passage calls them "careful observers".

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "discipline" most nearly means:
o: punishment for breaking rules
a branch of study such as biology
self-control in keeping to a careful method
obedience to a teacher's orders
x: "The discipline to change one thing at a time" means the self-control to keep strictly to a method. Punishment is a common meaning of the word, and a branch of study is another, but neither fits "the discipline to change".

q: In the third paragraph, the phrase "that single change" refers to:
o: the change that took place in the meat as it rotted
the critics' change of opinion about the test
the one way in which the jars were treated differently
the move from glass jars to cloth bags
x: The sentence says "Every jar was treated alike except in one respect", and "that single change" is that one respect, such as open versus covered. The rotting happened in every jar, so it was not the difference being tested.

q: Which of the following best describes the passage?
o: A teacher's warning about collecting stones on school trips
A pupil's find that leads to an account of how people explained shells found inland
A history of the great floods that once covered the Salt Range
A boy's argument with his teacher about how mountains are formed
x: Bilal's shell-marked stone leads Miss Kausar to describe the explanations people gave, ending with the idea that "the land itself had slowly risen". There is no argument between them: she answers his question.

q: According to the passage, what did some observers notice about the shells that argued against a flood?
o: They had grown inside the rock by themselves
They were scattered loosely over the surface
They lay in flat layers stacked one above another
They belonged to animals that live in rivers
x: The shells "lay in flat layers, one above another, like pages in a book, which is not how a sudden flood leaves things". Growing inside the rock was a different, earlier explanation, not an observation.

q: It can be inferred that Miss Kausar "did not answer at once" because she:
o: did not know the answer to the question herself
thought the question was too simple to discuss
wanted the class to see how the answer had been reached over time
wished to scold Bilal for picking up stones
x: Instead of answering, she tells how people "had been asking the same question for a very long time" and how each explanation was tested. She clearly knew the answer, since she goes on to explain it.

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "absurd" most nearly means:
o: ridiculous and impossible to believe
amusing and light-hearted
carefully argued and convincing
already known to everyone
x: The idea seemed "absurd" because "nobody had ever seen a mountain move", so it seemed impossible to believe. "Amusing" is a loose everyday sense of the word, but the people were doubting the idea, not laughing at a joke.

q: Which best describes Bilal's feeling about the stone at the end of the passage?
o: Disappointment that it was only an ordinary stone
A new sense of wonder at what it could tell him
Embarrassment at having asked a foolish question
Doubt that his teacher's account was true
x: Once "rubbish under his shoe", the stone now "felt like a message that had waited a very long time to be read". Disappointment is the opposite: the stone has become special to him.

q: What is the writer's main purpose in the passage?
o: To explain why wood leaves less ash than metal leaves powder
To argue that a mistaken theory can help science when it is tested
To criticise the chemists who believed in a hidden burning substance
To show that students should not study old theories at all
x: The writer says "a good wrong theory can do as much to move knowledge forward as a right one" and uses the burning theory as the example. The chemists are not criticised: they took the theory "seriously enough to test".

q: According to the passage, what did the old theory predict about a metal heated until it crumbled?
o: That it would leave only a little ash, as wood does
That the powder would weigh less than the metal
That the powder would weigh more than the metal
That it would take something from the air
x: The prediction was that the powder "should, having lost something, weigh less". That it weighed more was the result that the workers actually found, the opposite of the prediction.

q: The writer would most likely agree that a theory is most useful to science when it:
o: explains everything without needing to be checked
makes claims that experiments could show to be false
is accepted by most experts of its time
is correct from the very beginning
x: The burning theory proved useful because it "made a prediction that could be checked", and the writer says the real failure is "refusing to find out whether you are wrong". Being correct from the start is not required: the useful theory here was wrong.

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "tidy" most nearly means:
o: clean and well swept
small in size
neat and simple in its explanation
fully proven by tests
x: "The theory was tidy, and it explained a great deal": it was neat and simple. "Clean and well swept" is the word's meaning for a room, not for a theory.

q: Which best describes the writer's attitude towards the old theory of burning?
o: Scornful, treating it as a foolish obstacle
Convinced that it was mostly correct
Indifferent, seeing it as unimportant
Respectful of its usefulness even though it was wrong
x: The writer calls it "tidy", says it "explained a great deal" and credits it with opening "the way to a new understanding of chemistry". Scorn is wrong: the writer objects to treating wrong ideas "as if they had been nothing but obstacles".

q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
o: Roundabouts are safer than traffic lights and should replace them everywhere
Traffic lights waste fuel and should be switched off at night
Lights and roundabouts each have strengths and weaknesses, so the choice depends on the crossing
Pedestrians cannot cross safely at any kind of roundabout
x: The passage weighs both tools and ends "Neither tool, then, is simply better. The right choice depends on how much traffic arrives". Roundabouts are not said to be better everywhere: "roundabouts have limits too".

q: According to the passage, why are violent crashes rare at roundabouts?
o: Pedestrians are kept away from the circle
Drivers wait for a light before they enter
Traffic from each road enters in strict turn
Every vehicle has to slow down and turn
x: The third paragraph says "Because every vehicle must slow down and turn, the violent head-on and side impacts ... become rare". Waiting for a light and taking turns describe traffic lights, not roundabouts.

q: It can be inferred that traffic lights would be the better choice for a crossing:
o: beside a school where many children cross on foot
on a quiet road where cars arrive only now and then
where engineers want drivers to judge gaps for themselves
where the main aim is to save fuel late at night
x: Signals "suit crossings where pedestrians need a protected moment to cross", while "a large roundabout can be hard for people on foot". A quiet road is where lights are weakest: drivers sit "facing an empty junction".

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "glancing" most nearly means:
o: striking at an angle rather than head-on
looking quickly at something
shining with a sudden light
happening by pure chance
x: "Glancing" collisions are set against "violent head-on and side impacts", so they strike at an angle and slide off. "Looking quickly" is the common meaning of glance, not the one used for a collision.

q: How does the third paragraph relate to the second?
o: It gives an example that supports the claim made in the second paragraph
It treats the other tool in the same way, giving its benefits and then its limits
It corrects a mistake in the second paragraph's account of signals
It explains why the tool described in the second paragraph was invented
x: The second paragraph gives the strengths of lights and then "Their weakness"; the third, opening "by contrast", gives the strengths of roundabouts and then "roundabouts have limits too". It does not correct the second paragraph, which it leaves standing.

q: What does the passage mainly explain?
o: Why goods trains need more powerful engines than lorries
How rubber tyres were improved for use on railways
Why railway lines are always built through tunnels
How the hardness of wheel and rail makes trains efficient but also limits them
x: The second paragraph explains the efficiency of "steel on steel" and the third the "drawback" of the same hardness. Engine power is played down: the secret lies "not so much in the engine's power".

q: According to the passage, why does a lorry lose more energy in rolling than a train?
o: Its tyres keep flattening and springing back as they turn
Its wheels touch the road over a patch no larger than a coin
Its engine is much smaller than a locomotive's
It has to stop more often on busy roads
x: A rubber tyre "flattens slightly ... and springs back", and "That constant squashing and recovering uses up energy". The coin-sized patch describes the steel wheel on the rail, not the lorry.

q: Which of the following is best supported by the reasoning of the passage?
o: A lorry carrying the same load would use less fuel than the train
A steel train wheel wears out faster than a rubber tyre
A train driver must start braking much earlier than a lorry driver at the same speed
A train can climb any slope if its engine is powerful enough
x: Steel on steel gives "little grip", so a train "needs a long distance to stop" and signals must warn drivers "well in advance"; a rubber tyre, which does not slide so easily, can stop sooner. Fuel is the reverse: rail takes "far less fuel for each tonne".

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "gradients" most nearly means:
o: gradual changes of colour
bends to the left or right
slopes of the ground
levels of difficulty
x: Trains cannot climb "steep slopes", so engineers lay tracks along "gentle gradients", that is, gentle slopes. Bends are a different thing: the lines "curve around hills" to avoid steep gradients.

q: The word "however" in the first sentence of the third paragraph shows that the writer is about to:
o: give another example of the same advantage
repeat the main point of the first paragraph
describe the early history of the railway
turn from an advantage of steel to a drawback
x: "However" marks a contrast: after the efficiency of steel on steel, "The same hardness ... brings a drawback", the lack of grip. It does not add another advantage.

q: Which of the following would be the most suitable title for the passage?
o: A Road Full of New Signs
Why Night Buses Are Dangerous
Cotton Fields at Dawn
The Man Who Stayed Awake
x: The passage centres on Akram, and the narrator concludes that "Forty people had slept safely because one man stayed awake and paid attention". The road signs and the cotton fields are small details.

q: According to the passage, why did Akram distrust the new road signs?
o: They were too dim to read in the dark
They showed how the road ought to be, not how it was that night
They had been put up in the wrong places
They distracted drivers from watching for cattle
x: Akram says the signs "tell you what the road should be, ... not what it is tonight". He does not say they are dim: the passage calls them "bright new road signs".

q: The passage suggests that most of the passengers did not know that:
o: the driver had skilfully avoided a dangerous truck
the bus had arrived in Multan late
the narrator had been given the driver's seat
the bus had taken a different road from usual
x: Akram passed the truck "so smoothly that most of the passengers never woke", and at Multan "Hardly anyone looked back at the driver". Nothing in the passage says the bus was late or changed its road.

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "loomed" most nearly means:
o: was woven on a frame
moved slowly away
flashed its lights brightly
appeared suddenly as a large, threatening shape
x: A truck "without tail-lights loomed out of the dark": it rose up suddenly, big and dangerous. Weaving on a frame belongs to the noun "loom", and nothing in the sentence suggests flashing lights.

q: By the end of the passage, the narrator's attitude towards Akram is best described as:
o: mild annoyance at his long silence
pity for the tiring job he does
amusement at his old-fashioned habits
grateful respect for his quiet skill
x: The narrator credits Akram with the safety of forty people and is the one passenger who looks back, sharing a sign "as if we had shared a secret". Annoyance belongs only to the first hour, when he "assumed" Akram resented him.

q: The writer's main purpose in the passage is to:
o: explain how shopkeepers can attract more customers to their shops
argue that charging for street parking would make busy streets work better
argue that cars should be kept out of market streets altogether
describe how cities decide where to build new car parks
x: The writer argues that free parking causes crowding and that "A modest charge ... would change behaviour". Banning cars is wrong: the charge works "without banning anyone" and "None of this is a war on motorists".

q: According to the passage, who often fills the spaces outside shops on a street with free parking?
o: Customers making quick visits to the shops
Delivery vans unloading goods for the market
A few early arrivals, sometimes the shopkeepers themselves
Fruit sellers with their carts
x: The spaces "are often filled all day by a few early arrivals, sometimes the shopkeepers themselves". Quick visits are what a charge would make room for, not what happens now.

q: The writer's argument implies that the main cost of free parking falls on:
o: drivers, who must buy extra fuel while circling
the town, which must pay to build new car parks
shopkeepers, who must pay rent for the spaces outside
people who could have used the street space in other ways
x: Someone pays for the space, "only not the driver": the land could have held a footpath, a cart, a bus stop or trees, and pedestrians "have long been denied" good pavements. Drivers are wrong because the writer says plainly that they are not the ones who pay.

q: As used in the first paragraph, the word "curious" most nearly means:
o: eager to learn or know
carefully made
kind and generous
strange and unusual
x: A gift that is paid for by someone other than the giver or the receiver is a "curious kind of gift", that is, a strange one. "Eager to learn" is the commoner meaning, used of people, not of a gift.

q: Which best describes the writer's tone in the last paragraph?
o: Angry and hostile towards car owners
Doubtful and hesitant about the proposal
Reasonable and reassuring, stressing that the plan is fair
Playful, making jokes about drivers
x: The writer calls the charge "modest", says "None of this is a war on motorists" and asks only for "a fair share". Hostility is ruled out by that very sentence about motorists.

q: Which statement best sums up the passage?
o: Muscle soreness shows that a person has exercised in the wrong way
Delayed soreness comes from small injuries that the body repairs and learns to resist
Acid left in the muscles causes pain that lasts for several days
Downhill running should be avoided by all beginners
x: The passage traces the ache to "tiny tears in muscle fibres" and says it is "mostly a sign of adaptation". The acid idea is the one the passage rejects: it "does not fit the timing".

q: According to the passage, which kind of movement causes the most damage to muscle fibres?
o: One done very quickly with no load at all
One in which the muscle lengthens as it works
One in which the muscle holds a weight without moving
One repeated many times on level ground
x: "The damage is greatest in movements where a muscle lengthens while it works, such as lowering a heavy load". Holding a weight still is not mentioned.

q: The passage suggests that walking down a steep hill is likely to cause more soreness than walking up it because:
o: going down produces more acid in the muscles
walking uphill tears more of the muscle fibres
going down makes the leg muscles lengthen while they work
going down is faster and so tires the heart
x: Walking downhill is given as an example of a muscle that "lengthens while it works", the movement that does the most damage. Acid is wrong because the passage says acid does not cause the ache at all.

q: As used in the first paragraph, the word "ordeal" most nearly means:
o: a formal ceremony
a painful and difficult experience
an exciting challenge
a short delay
x: When soreness arrives, "climbing stairs becomes an ordeal" and sitting is "a careful, groaning business", so the word means a painful, hard experience. Nothing in it is exciting.

q: What is the main function of the second paragraph?
o: It describes how soreness can be prevented by gradual training
It lists the symptoms that soreness produces
It defends the belief that acid causes soreness
It rejects a common explanation and offers a better-supported one
x: It opens "That explanation does not fit the timing" and then gives the view that soreness comes "from tiny tears in muscle fibres". Gradual training is the advice of the third paragraph.

q: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?
o: Loud coaches teach young players more than quiet ones
A coach taught most effectively by letting the narrator discover a lesson himself
Keeping the head still is the most important skill in bowling
The narrator nearly left the club because of an unfriendly coach
x: The lessons "that stayed with me were the ones Master Yousaf let me find for myself". The narrator says he learned from louder coaches "too", but less lastingly, so they did not teach him more.

q: What did the narrator discover during the practice with the cup?
o: The cup had been placed too far away to be hit
His good deliveries came when he kept his head still as he let go of the ball
Most of his good balls went down the leg side
He bowled better when the coach stood close by
x: He noticed that "the good ones came when I kept my head still at the moment of release". It was most of his poor balls, not the good ones, that "sprayed down the leg side".

q: The narrator's belief after the first evening that the coach had "already written me off" proved to be:
o: correct, since the coach never gave him any help
correct, because the coach preferred louder players
wrong, as the coach's later attention showed
wrong, because the coach praised him that same evening
x: The next week the coach set him a task, smiled at his discovery and said "Good", so he had not given up on him. The coach did not praise him on the first evening; he only "nodded, and walked away".

q: As used in the first paragraph, the phrase "written me off" most nearly means:
o: put my name on the team list
decided I was not worth bothering with
sent me a letter of refusal
noted my mistakes on paper
x: After the coach "nodded, and walked away", the narrator feared he had been judged worthless, which is what "written me off" means. Nothing was literally written, so the letter and the paper notes are wrong.

q: Looking back as an adult, how does the narrator regard Master Yousaf's silence?
o: He resents it as a lack of interest in young players
He finds it amusing but of little real use
He values it as a wise way of teaching and tries to copy it
He regrets that it kept him from learning more
x: He calls it "his patient silence" and, when coaching boys of his own, says "I remember that cup, and I keep quiet a little longer". Resentment is wrong: the lessons it gave are the ones that "stayed with me".

q: What is the writer's main argument?
o: Rest is an essential part of training, because the body improves during recovery
Athletes should give up hard training and rely on gentle movement
Coaches are mainly to blame for injuries among young athletes
Sleep matters more than training for success in sport
x: The writer says "The improvement comes afterwards, during recovery" and calls rest "the half of training that nobody sees". Hard training is not given up: it is "the signal" that rest answers.

q: According to the passage, how does hard training affect performance the next morning?
o: It makes the athlete stronger at once
It often makes performance worse, as the muscles are tired
It has no effect until a week has passed
It improves speed but weakens strength
x: Hard training "leaves muscles tired and slightly damaged, and performance the next morning is often worse". It does not make a person stronger "on the day it is done".

q: The writer would most likely disapprove of an athlete who:
o: takes a rest day with a short walk and an early night
trains hard every day and feels guilty about taking a day off
trains hard on some days and gently on others
eats a proper meal after a hard session
x: The writer criticises the view that rest days are "something to apologise for" and that training "every day without a break" shows dedication. A walk and an early night fit the advice: "Gentle movement, good sleep and proper meals are part of the work".

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "nagging" most nearly means:
o: complaining and scolding
sudden and severe
slight and harmless
persistent and troublesome
x: "Nagging injuries" come with "heavy legs" and "falling times": they keep troubling the athlete. "Complaining and scolding" is the word's meaning for a person, not for an injury.

q: The tone of the passage as a whole is best described as:
o: light and humorous, poking fun at athletes
uncertain, unable to decide between two views
firm and corrective, challenging a common belief
bitter, blaming coaches for harming athletes
x: The writer states plainly that the usual attitude "misunderstands how the body improves" and that athletes "need to stop treating recovery as time lost". Coaches are mentioned without bitterness, alongside the athletes themselves.

q: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
o: Team and individual sports teach different lessons, so the choice should suit the child
Team games are better than individual sports for every child
Individual sports are too harsh for children to enjoy
Parents should let children change sports often
x: The passage says the two kinds "teach different lessons" and ends "Wise parents therefore look less at the sport and more at the child". Neither kind is said to be better for every child.

q: According to the passage, what is one drawback of team games?
o: Players are blamed personally for every defeat
Players are rarely helped by their teammates
Winners cannot share the credit with others
A quiet child may take little part and never find out what he or she can do
x: "A quiet child can hide in a team, touching the ball rarely and never quite discovering what he or she can do". Personal blame for failure is a feature of individual sports, not team games.

q: It can be inferred that, in the writer's view, the chance to hide that a team offers is:
o: a serious fault that makes team games useless
both a comfort for some children and a limit on others
an advantage with no real drawback
something found only in football and hockey
x: The second paragraph treats hiding as a disadvantage, yet the last says "A shy child might flourish when carried along by a team". It is not a fault that makes team games useless, since they teach "a lesson in belonging".

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "glamorous" most nearly means:
o: attractive and likely to win attention
fashionably dressed
difficult and tiring
important for winning
x: A role "that may not be glamorous" is one that brings little attention, like defending while others score. "Fashionably dressed" is the word's common meaning, but the sentence is about a role, not clothes.

q: How does the last paragraph relate to the second and third paragraphs?
o: It gives a new example of an individual sport
It contradicts what they say about team games
It repeats their points without adding anything
It draws practical advice from the comparison they set out
x: The second and third paragraphs compare the two kinds of sport; the last begins "Wise parents therefore" and turns the comparison into advice about the child. It agrees with them rather than contradicting them.

q: What does the passage mainly describe?
o: How making a field level helps farmers use water evenly and well
How lasers are used to measure the size of farms
Why oxen have been replaced by tractors on farms
How farmers can store water in the low corners of fields
x: The passage explains the waste on an uneven field, how laser levelling "solves this", and its other "benefits". Water lying in low corners is the problem, not a way of storing it.

q: According to the passage, what happens when water flows across a field that is higher at one end?
o: It spreads evenly but sinks too quickly
It washes soil from the low corners to the high ones
It collects in the low parts while the high patches stay dry
It flows back into the channel
x: "The water races to the low corners and lies there in pools, while the high patches stay dry". It does not spread evenly; even wetting is what levelling achieves.

q: The passage suggests that a farmer who keeps watering an uneven field is likely to:
o: need less fertiliser than a farmer with a level field
use more water and harvest a crop that ripens unevenly
harvest the whole crop on a single day
need to rent a laser-guided tractor every week
x: On an uneven field water must run "far longer than the crop needs", and since an evenly wetted field makes the crop ripen "together", an uneven one will not. Less fertiliser is wrong: on uneven ground it is "washed into the hollows".

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "plane" most nearly means:
o: an aircraft in flight
a tool for smoothing wood
a narrow beam of light
a flat, even surface
x: "The beam marks a perfectly level plane", a flat surface that the scraper follows. A wood-smoothing tool also shaves, but here the scraper does the shaving; the plane is the level it is guided to.

q: In the last paragraph, the phrase "such equipment" refers to:
o: the laser-guided tractor and scraper
the wooden board dragged behind oxen
the channels that carry water to the field
the fertiliser spread on the crop
x: The equipment that small farmers cannot buy, and so rent "for a day", is the tractor with the laser-guided scraper. The wooden board was the old, cheap method used "In the past".

q: Which would be the best title for the passage?
o: How Bricks Are Made in a Village
The Last Farm on the Channel
A Quarrel Between Neighbours
Learning to Farm Without Water
x: The passage is about the narrator's family at "the very end of a long watercourse" and how lining the channel changed their Thursday nights. There is no quarrel: the father was "never shouting at anyone".

q: According to the narrator, why did so little water reach his family's fields?
o: Their turn was shorter than that of other families
The channel had been lined with bricks too late
Their fields lay higher than the rest of the farms
Some soaked into the banks and some was taken by neighbours upstream
x: Water "had soaked into the earth banks" and "had been quietly taken by neighbours who left their outlets open". Their turn was not shorter: it "lasted as many hours as anyone's".

q: The narrator's boyhood view that the system was fair overlooked the fact that:
o: his family had a longer turn than other farmers
the turns were fixed by his father alone
Thursday nights were the busiest time on the channel
equal hours of water did not mean equal amounts of water
x: As a boy he reasoned "Each family had its turn", but later saw that, though their turn "lasted as many hours as anyone's", the stream was "thin and tired". A longer turn is contradicted by that same sentence.

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "tired" most nearly means:
o: weakened after flowing so far
in need of sleep
bored and uninterested
dirty with mud
x: After passing "thirty farms", the stream was "thin and tired", that is, weak and reduced, in contrast to the "fast and clear" water that comes later. "In need of sleep" is the everyday meaning, used of people.

q: What does the father's going to bed early at the end of the passage most likely show?
o: Relief that he no longer had to guard the water
Anger at the cost of the brick lining
Disappointment with the new channel
Illness after years of hard work
x: For years he spent Thursday nights "walking the channel with a lantern"; now the water arrives "fast and clear", so he can rest. Disappointment is wrong: the work has solved his problem.

q: What is the main point of the passage?
o: Farmers should stop buying modern seed from shops
Village seed banks keep local varieties whose qualities may one day be needed
Old local varieties always give heavier yields
Seed banks need large buildings to work well
x: The passage describes village seed banks and says "they keep choices open" for a year "of drought or a new disease". Giving up modern seed is wrong: the banks "are no argument against modern seed".

q: According to the passage, how is the stock of a village seed bank kept fresh?
o: The seed is sealed in tins and never opened
New seed is bought from shops every year
Farmers borrow seed and return more after the harvest
Old seed is thrown away after one season
x: "A farmer may borrow a few kilograms at sowing time and return a larger amount after the harvest, so the stock is renewed". Sealed tins are mentioned, but only as containers.

q: The passage suggests that a local variety is most likely to be lost when:
o: it is stored in a labelled clay pot
farmers stop resowing it because a higher-yielding seed is easy to buy
a drought shows how valuable it is
a family lends some of it to a neighbour
x: Local varieties survived because they were "saved and resown by families over generations"; they are disappearing now that seed "comes from a shop" with "heavier yields". Storing seed in a pot is how the banks keep it, not how it is lost.

q: As used in the first paragraph, the word "traits" most nearly means:
o: habits of a person's character
goods offered for sale
qualities that a plant has
marks left by a disease
x: The "traits" are then listed: surviving frost, ripening on little rain, being ignored by pests, all qualities of a crop. Habits of character is the meaning used for people, not plants.

q: The writer's attitude towards modern shop-bought seed is best described as:
o: strongly hostile, wishing it banned
wholly enthusiastic, seeing no drawbacks
accepting of its benefits while warning of what is being lost
uninterested, since it hardly matters
x: The writer grants that new varieties "often give heavier yields" but says "something has been lost in the change". Hostility is wrong: the banks "are no argument against modern seed".

q: Which title would suit the passage best?
o: Why Orchards Hire Bees
How Bees Make Honey from Nectar
The Dangers of Spraying Fruit Trees
Why Wind Is the Orchard's Best Friend
x: The passage explains why owners rent hives "while the trees are in flower" and how the arrangement works. Spraying is only one condition of the deal, and wind "does little of this work".

q: According to the passage, why do some large orchards need hired bees?
o: They have too few wild insects to visit every blossom in time
Their trees make no pollen of their own
The wind carries too much of their pollen away
Their owners want to sell honey
x: Large orchards "often have too few wild insects to visit every blossom in the short time the trees are in flower". The honey goes to the beekeepers, not the orchard owners.

q: It can be inferred that a small orchard surrounded by hedges and wild flowers:
o: needs more hired hives than a large orchard
cannot be pollinated by insects at all
may produce a good crop without hired hives
must never be sprayed at any time of year
x: Large orchards lack insects because they have "few hedges or wild flowers nearby", and "Where wild insects are plentiful, an orchard may need no help". The passage warns only against spraying "while the trees are in bloom", not all year.

q: As used in the first paragraph, the word "cargo" most nearly means:
o: a load being carried
a kind of ship
a type of fruit
a payment for rent
x: The "strange cargo" is the boxes of bees "stacked on the backs of pick-up trucks", a load being carried. The rent is paid for the bees; it is not the cargo itself.

q: In the last paragraph, the phrase "the visitors" refers to:
o: the orchard owners
the pests on the trees
the beekeepers who bring the hives
the hired bees
x: The bees are brought in for a few weeks, and if the trees are sprayed "the visitors will die along with the pests". The pests cannot be meant, since the visitors die "along with" them.

q: What is the passage mainly concerned with?
o: How pots are fired and cooled in a kiln
Why beginners should not use a potter's wheel
Why centring the clay is an essential first step in throwing a pot
How potters decorate the walls of a pot
x: The passage says centring "decides whether everything that follows will succeed" and explains what goes wrong without it and how it is done. The kiln is mentioned only as a place where a badly centred pot may crack.

q: According to the passage, why does a wobble grow if it is not corrected?
o: The high side is pushed harder each time it passes the fingers
The wheel slows down as the clay dries
The clay becomes heavier on its low side
Water collects on one side of the lump
x: "Each time the high side passes the potter's fingers, it is pushed harder than the low side, so the wobble grows". Nothing is said about the wheel slowing down.

q: The lesson that apprentices say "applies well beyond the wheel" is most likely that:
o: steady patience often achieves more than force
clay must always be kept wet
every task should be finished within one minute
skilled workers should not teach beginners
x: The lesson is the one just described: beginners "fight the clay, gripping hard", while experienced potters "hold still and steady and let the clay come to them". The "first minute" in the opening describes how centring looks, not a rule.

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "true" most nearly means:
o: honestly, without lying
loyally and faithfully
quickly, at full speed
evenly and accurately, without wobbling
x: Centring forces the clay "to run true", the opposite of the wobble described before: it turns evenly round the centre. "Honestly" is the word's common meaning, used of people and statements.

q: What does the second paragraph mainly do?
o: It describes how a beginner learns to centre the clay
It gives the history of the potter's wheel
It shows how a pot is decorated before firing
It explains what goes wrong if the clay is not centred
x: It describes a lump "even slightly off-centre" that wobbles and gives a pot uneven walls that "collapse" or "crack". How centring is done comes in the third paragraph.

q: Which statement best describes what the passage is about?
o: An aunt's anger at a niece who wasted cloth
The history of block printing in the town of Hala
How wooden blocks are carved into patterns of leaves
A girl's struggle with a craft and her discovery that skill means doing it again and again
x: The narrator spoils cloth, finally makes a clean print and understands that "a whole cloth of them would be skill". The aunt shows no anger: she "said nothing" and handed the block back.

q: According to the passage, what happened when the narrator pressed a pale patch a second time?
o: The block cracked under the extra pressure
The dye ran off the edges of the cloth
The outline was doubled and the cloth was spoiled
The colour became too dark to use
x: Pressing again, she "doubled the outline and spoiled the whole length of cloth". Nothing is said about the block cracking.

q: The aunt's habit of saying nothing and handing back the block suggests that she:
o: had lost interest in teaching her niece
expected mistakes as a normal part of learning
thought the narrator would never learn
wanted her to try a different pattern
x: She "simply laid out another strip" each time, and when a good print came she set the next task, "Now do it four hundred more times". Losing interest is wrong: she kept supplying cloth for a whole week.

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "whole" most nearly means:
o: healthy and free from illness
large and spread out
joined to the other prints
complete, with no part missing
x: The leaves sat on the cloth "sharp and dark and whole", unlike the earlier prints that were "blurred at one edge and pale at the other". "Healthy" is an old sense of the word, used of people.

q: What does the narrator's laughter at the end of the passage most likely show?
o: Pleasure that her aunt had praised her at last
Relief that her training was now over
Scorn for her aunt's refusal to praise her
Good-humoured acceptance that one success is only a beginning
x: She laughs "but I understood": "One good print was luck; a whole cloth of them would be skill". Relief is wrong, since the aunt has just given her four hundred more prints to make.

q: What is the main idea of the passage?
o: Glue matters more than the cut of the wood
A carpenter must understand the grain of wood to make work that is strong and lasts
Fresh wood is stronger than dried wood
Firewood should always be cut along the grain
x: The passage shows how grain decides where wood is strong and how it shrinks, and why careful carpenters respect both. Glue is wrong: a carpenter looks first at "not the joint or the glue but the grain".

q: According to the passage, how does wood shrink as it dries?
o: Equally in every direction
Much more across the grain than along it
Much more along the grain than across it
Only around the joints
x: It shrinks "not evenly: far more across the grain than along it". Shrinking more along the grain is the reverse of what the passage says.

q: The final sentence of the passage suggests that a carpenter who ignores how wood behaves will:
o: sooner or later see the work fail
save time and money in the long run
be able to hide the faults with stronger glue
need to buy more firewood
x: "Impatience is costly in this trade; the wood will always have the last word": the wood's nature wins in the end, as in the table that cracks "a few months later". Saving money is contradicted by "costly".

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "load" most nearly means:
o: the weight or force a part must bear
goods carried by a lorry
a large amount of work
the charge put into a gun
x: Each part is cut so its grain "follows the direction of the load it must carry", such as the weight on a chair leg. Goods on a lorry is a common meaning, but nothing is being transported here.

q: The words "Grain matters for another reason" at the start of the third paragraph show that the writer is:
o: moving from the strength of wood to the way it shrinks
repeating the point about chair legs in other words
turning to argue against the first two paragraphs
giving an example of how firewood is cut
x: The first two paragraphs are about strength along the grain; the third turns to drying, where wood shrinks "far more across the grain than along it". It adds a second reason rather than arguing against the first.

q: The passage is mainly concerned with:
o: how weavers can gain a fairer share of what their work earns
why city shops charge too much for shawls
the history of shawl weaving in villages
why traders should be driven out of weaving villages
x: The passage describes the weaver's small share and argues that cooperatives can pay her "something close to what their work is worth". Driving out traders is rejected: without a replacement "she would be worse off".

q: According to the passage, why does the weaver depend on the trader?
o: He pays her more than city shops would
He gives her yarn and buyers she cannot reach on her own
He owns the loom she works on
He trains her to weave new designs
x: She "has no other way to buy yarn in bulk, no means of reaching distant buyers and no savings to wait". He does not pay more than shops: the shop price is "several times as much".

q: The writer would most likely agree that simply driving traders out of weaving villages would:
o: make the weavers rich at once
make no difference to the weavers' earnings
harm the weavers unless something else took over the trader's role
force city shops to lower their prices
x: "Take away the trader without replacing what he provides, and she would be worse off", and the cooperative is the replacement the writer proposes. Nothing suggests they would grow rich at once; the writer says the opposite.

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "symptom" most nearly means:
o: a feeling of illness in the body
the main cause of a difficulty
a sign of a deeper problem rather than its cause
a dishonest person who cheats others
x: The trader is "a symptom more than a cause": he exists because of the weaver's deeper lack of yarn, buyers and savings. "The main cause" is the opposite of what the sentence says.

q: Which best describes the writer's attitude towards weavers' cooperatives?
o: Doubtful that any of them can ever succeed
Uncritically enthusiastic, seeing no difficulties
Hopeful but realistic about how hard they are to run
Dismissive, regarding them as a form of charity
x: The writer calls them "The more useful answer" but admits they need "patience, honest bookkeeping" and "many fail". Charity is ruled out by the words "not charity".

q: The passage mainly explains:
o: why small birds leave cold countries every autumn
how bright city lights have changed the routes birds take
how birds combine several different guides to find their way on long journeys
why pilots should always carry more than one instrument
x: The second paragraph says birds "do not rely on a single guide but carry several", and the rest shows why that makes them "so dependable". The pilot is only a comparison, not the subject.

q: According to the second paragraph, what seems to tell birds which way is north when clouds hide the sun and the stars?
o: The movement of the sun across the sky
The pattern of stars around the pole
A sense of the earth's magnetism
The lights of towns below them
x: The passage says "When clouds hide both, a sense of the earth's magnetism seems to tell them which way is north." The sun and the stars are the very guides the clouds have hidden.

q: Suppose a bird somehow lost its magnetic sense but flew under clear skies. The passage suggests it would most likely:
o: be unable to tell which way is north
still find its way by using the sun and the stars
have to find its way by smell alone
be drawn off course by city lights
x: Because birds carry several guides, one lost guide matters little: the bird "simply leans more heavily on whichever cues remain", and the sun and stars are available on clear days and nights. Being unable to find north contradicts this point about redundancy.

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "redundancy" most nearly means:
o: the loss of a job because a worker is no longer needed
having spare guides that can do the same job
a long period of rest before a journey
the habit of returning to the same place
x: The pilot "with four" instruments "can afford to lose one", so redundancy here means having spare means that can do the same job. Losing one's job is the word's commoner meaning, not the one used here.

q: The third paragraph mainly serves to:
o: describe how pilots are trained to fly through storms
introduce a new guide that birds use near home
show that birds usually get lost in bad weather
explain, through a comparison, why having several guides makes the system reliable
x: It opens "This redundancy is what makes the system so dependable" and compares birds with a pilot who "can afford to lose one" instrument. It does not say birds usually get lost; the last paragraph says most journeys end "where it should".

q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
o: Owls hunt mainly at dusk because mice are easier to find then
Engineers have built wind turbines that are quieter than any bird
Special features of its feathers let the owl fly almost silently, at some cost
Owls are faster fliers than falcons and pigeons
x: The passage explains the "three unusual ways" the feathers are shaped, then what "These features cost the owl". Owls being faster than falcons is contradicted: the feathers "do not allow the bursts of speed that a falcon achieves".

q: What, according to the passage, does the velvety down on the upper surface of the feathers do?
o: It softens the sound of feathers rubbing together
It keeps rain from soaking into the wings
It breaks the air into many small streams
It lets air leave the wing without a sudden snap
x: The down "muffles the rub of feather against feather as the wing beats". Breaking the air into streams is the job of the leading-edge fringes, and the soft trailing edge stops the "single noisy wave".

q: The passage suggests that silent flight matters to the owl mainly because:
o: it lets the owl fly faster than other birds
it keeps the owl's feathers dry in the rain
other owls would otherwise compete for the same mouse
its prey would otherwise hear it coming and escape
x: The owl "can glide within a metre of a mouse without being heard" while hunting, so silence lets it get close to prey unnoticed. Speed is wrong: the owl has "traded speed" for stealth.

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "traded" most nearly means:
o: given up in exchange
bought and sold for money
carried over long distances
compared carefully
x: The owl loses speed and weatherproofing and gains stealth, so "traded ... for" means gave up one thing to get another. Buying and selling is the everyday meaning, but no money is involved here.

q: How does the third paragraph relate to the second?
o: It points out the disadvantages that come with the features just described
It gives further examples of how the feathers reduce noise
It describes how engineers copied the owl's feathers
It casts doubt on the claim that owls fly silently
x: The second paragraph lists the three feather features; the third begins "These features cost the owl something" and names rain and lost speed. Engineers copying the design come only in the fourth paragraph.

q: The passage is mainly concerned with:
o: why lakes in Gilgit-Baltistan freeze harder than lakes elsewhere
how wax and water behave in the same way as they cool
how an unusual property of water lets fish survive under frozen lakes
why fish prefer very cold water to warm water
x: The passage explains "an odd habit of water" and ends that this "quirk" "makes winter life in cold lakes possible". Wax is the contrast, not a match: water behaves like it "only down to about four degrees".

q: What happens once the whole lake has cooled to about four degrees?
o: The coldest water sinks to the bottom and freezes there
Warm water rises from the lakebed and melts the surface
Water at the surface keeps cooling but stays on top because it is lighter
The whole lake turns to ice at the same moment
x: The second paragraph says "After that, the surface water cools further but, being lighter, stays on top. It freezes there". Ice piling up on the lakebed is what would happen only if water behaved "like wax".

q: The passage suggests that if ice were a good conductor of heat, the water beneath it would:
o: stay at a steady four degrees all winter
lose its warmth faster, so more of the lake might freeze
rise to the surface and melt the ice
become warmer than it is in summer
x: The ice protects the water because it is "a poor conductor of heat", "slowing the loss of warmth from the water below"; a good conductor would let that warmth escape faster. A steady temperature is what the poor conductor provides, so it would no longer be assured.

q: As used in the last paragraph, the word "quirk" most nearly means:
o: a serious fault
a strict rule
an odd feature
a lucky accident
x: The "quirk" is the "odd habit of water" described at the start, so it means an odd feature. It is not called a fault; it is what makes life possible.

q: At the start of the third paragraph, the words "That lid" refer to:
o: the layer of water at about four degrees
the warmer water rising from below
the layer of ice formed on the surface of the lake
the mud on the bed of the lake
x: The second paragraph ends with the surface water that "freezes there, forming a lid", and the third goes on: "Ice is a poor conductor". The four-degree water is what lies beneath the lid.

q: The main purpose of the passage is to:
o: describe the Thar desert at different times of day
explain why the colour of the sky changes as the sun goes down
warn that dust and smoke make the evening air unhealthy
show that the air itself turns red in the evening
x: The passage says "what has changed is the length of the path that sunlight takes" and explains the blue noon sky and red sunset. The air turning red is denied at once: "The air has not changed colour".

q: Which light, according to the passage, is scattered most strongly by the particles of gas?
o: Red light, which has longer waves
White light coming straight from the sun
Orange light reflected by dust
Blue light, which has shorter waves
x: The second paragraph says "blue light, with its shorter waves, is scattered far more strongly than red". Red light is the one that passes "through more easily".

q: On an evening when the air is unusually clean and still, the passage suggests the sunset would most likely be:
o: blue instead of red
exactly as vivid as one after a windy day
impossible to see at all
less vivid than one after a dry, windy day
x: Dust and smoke "can deepen the effect", and "the most vivid sunsets follow a dry, windy day", so clean, still air would give a less vivid sunset. It would still be red, since the long path through the air scatters the blue away in any case.

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "geometry" most nearly means:
o: the branch of mathematics that studies shapes
the chemical make-up of the air
the angle of the sun and the path its light takes
the colour of the evening light
x: The sentence goes on "The sun sits low, and its light must slant through a much thicker slice of atmosphere", so geometry refers to the angle and route of the light. The branch of mathematics is the usual meaning, not the one here.

q: The final paragraph mainly serves to:
o: introduce a second cause of red sunsets
cast doubt on the explanation given earlier
describe the mountains around the Thar
apply the same explanation to a different everyday sight
x: "The same rule explains why distant mountains often look bluish": air between viewer and slopes adds "its own faint blue glow", which is the scattering already explained. It supports the earlier explanation rather than questioning it.

q: The passage is mainly about:
o: why reinforced concrete is the best material for every home
low-cost ways of making village houses less likely to collapse in earthquakes
how engineers predict when earthquakes will strike
why stone houses in the mountains last only a few years
x: After describing why stone houses fall, the passage gives "cheaper ways to hold a building together". Concrete is called "out of reach for most families", and stone houses stand "for decades".

q: Why, according to the passage, do the stone houses described fail in a strong earthquake?
o: Their roofs are too light to hold the walls in place
The ground beneath them sinks during the shaking
The quake pushes them sideways and their loosely joined walls come apart
Years of ordinary use have already cracked their walls
x: A quake "pushes it sideways, back and forth, and the loose walls simply peel apart". The roofs are "thick" and "heavy", not light.

q: The remark that "concrete poorly made can be deadlier than stone" suggests that:
o: stone is always a safer material than concrete
concrete should never be used in mountain villages
families prefer stone because it looks traditional
a stronger material is of little help unless it is used with skill
x: The danger lies in concrete "poorly made", so the material is only as good as the work. "Always safer" goes too far: the passage calls concrete "the obvious answer" and objects only to its cost and to bad workmanship.

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "modest" most nearly means:
o: shy about one's own success
limited in what it tries to do
cheap and poorly made
kept quiet or secret
x: The aim is not a "quake-proof" house but one that stands "long enough for the people inside to get out", so modest means limited. Being shy about one's success is the word's commoner meaning for people.

q: In the first paragraph, the words "Such a house" refer to a house:
o: built entirely of reinforced concrete
of stacked stones and mud mortar with a thick, flat roof
with bands of timber running through its walls
already damaged by an earlier earthquake
x: The sentence before describes houses "made of heavy stones stacked with weak mud mortar and topped with a thick, flat roof". Timber bands are one of the improvements described later.

q: The writer's main purpose is to:
o: describe how satellites forecast the weather
explain the danger of debris in space and why it is hard to clear
argue that countries should stop launching satellites
explain how rockets carry satellites into orbit
x: The passage sets out "the worry" about collisions, the "remedies" being tried and "The deeper difficulty" of paying for them. It never calls for an end to launches.

q: Which of these is mentioned as a way of dealing with the problem?
o: Launching satellites at lower speeds
Painting satellites to protect them from fragments
Moving old satellites into the busiest orbits
Designing satellites to burn up in the atmosphere when they stop working
x: The third paragraph says satellites "are now designed to burn up in the atmosphere at the end of their working lives". Old satellites go to "graveyard" orbits "far from the crowded lanes", not the busiest ones.

q: Based on the last paragraph, a company might be unwilling to pay for cleaning space mainly because:
o: others who paid nothing would gain from it just as much
debris does no harm to its own satellites
every cleaning method has been shown not to work
the rubbish will soon burn up on its own
x: Cleaning "costs money while benefiting everyone, including those who paid nothing", so a payer gets no special return. The methods are not said to fail; none is "yet cheap enough to use widely".

q: As used in the second paragraph, the phrase "in principle" most nearly means:
o: as a matter of moral rule
with complete certainty
in theory, even if it may not happen in practice
at the very beginning
x: Debris "could, in principle, go on multiplying" describes something possible in theory, which the word "could" also signals. "With complete certainty" is too strong.

q: In the second paragraph, the word "This" in "This is the worry" refers to:
o: the way one collision creates fragments that can wreck other satellites
the cost of launching new satellites
the loss of a tool by an astronaut
the speed of a bullet fired from a rifle
x: The first paragraph ends with a fragment that can "wreck a working satellite" and a wreck that "becomes thousands of new fragments"; the next sentence explains "Every collision makes another collision more likely". The rifle bullet is only used to show the speed.

q: The writer's main aim in the passage is to:
o: warn that lift cables often snap in tall buildings
reassure readers that lifts are very safe by explaining how they are designed
explain how to escape from a lift stuck between floors
describe how electricity is used to power lifts
x: The passage answers the fear "What if the cable snaps?" by describing the several ropes, the governor and a brake that "fails safe". It says the fear "has been out of date for well over a century", not that cables often snap.

q: What does the governor do if the car begins to drop faster than a set limit?
o: It cuts off the electricity to the lift
It attaches an extra steel rope to the car
It lowers the car slowly to the ground floor
It makes clamps grip the rails along which the car runs
x: "The governor trips a pair of clamps fitted to the car. These grip the steel rails along which it runs". Nothing is said about cutting the power; the brake works without it.

q: If the power failed at the same moment as the ropes, the passage suggests the car would:
o: still be stopped, because the clamps need no electricity
fall freely, because the brake runs on electricity
keep moving until the power came back
be held up by the governor's own motor
x: The governor stops a car that drops too fast, and the clamps "need no electricity to work": "A power cut therefore does not disable the brake." Joining these, the car would still be stopped.

q: As used in the third paragraph, the phrase "fails safe" means that the design:
o: ends up in a safe state when something goes wrong
breaks down more often than other designs
never needs to be checked or repaired
can fail only in places where no one is hurt
x: The clamps "snap shut when released", so a fault such as "A power cut" leaves the car held where it is: failure leads to safety. Breaking down more often reads "fails" literally and ignores "safe".

q: What role does the first paragraph play in the passage?
o: It describes an accident that the passage goes on to explain
It gives the history of the first lifts
It presents a common fear that the rest of the passage answers
It admits the writer's own fear of lifts
x: It raises the question "What if the cable snaps?", and the following paragraphs explain why this fear is "out of date". No accident is described, and the unease belongs to "Many people", not the writer.

q: Which title best suits the passage?
o: How Telescopes Make Stars Look Larger
Two Ways to Tell Planets from Stars
Why the Air Above Us Never Rests
How the Ancients Named the Stars
x: The passage gives the twinkling test and "a second test" of slow movement, then says "together they let anyone ... tell a world from a sun". Telescopes do not make stars larger: a star "appears as a single point of light" even through one.

q: Why, according to the passage, does a planet usually shine steadily?
o: Its light does not have to pass through the air
The bending of light from the many points of its disc averages out
It is larger than any of the stars
It gives off a steady light of its own
x: The planet is "a tiny disc, made of countless points of light" and "the bends average out across the disc". Its light is still bent by the air: "Each point is bent by the air".

q: The passage suggests that a star seen through a large telescope would most likely:
o: appear as a disc and stop twinkling
still twinkle, because it would still appear as a single point
move against the other stars within a few weeks
shine more steadily than a planet does
x: A star "even through a large telescope ... appears as a single point of light", and it is the narrow single beam that makes it twinkle. Appearing as a disc is what a planet does, not a star.

q: As used in the second paragraph, the phrase "naked eye" refers to looking:
o: with the eyes half closed
without a telescope or other aid
in complete darkness
with an eye that has no protection from light
x: The planet "looks like a dot to the naked eye" but is "really a tiny disc", in contrast to looking "through a large telescope". The phrase means the unaided eye.

q: In the third paragraph, the words "this very habit" refer to:
o: the twinkling of stars near the horizon
the stars keeping their patterns from year to year
a planet's slow change of position against the stars
the steady glow of a planet
x: The sentence before says "a planet slowly changes its position against the background of stars", and the name "meaning wanderer, records this very habit". The stars keeping their patterns is the background, not the wandering.

q: The writer's main purpose in the passage is to:
o: argue that quiet, empty moments can be valuable for creative thought
persuade teenagers to give up their phones completely
explain why waiting rooms make people uncomfortable
describe how earlier generations spent their free time
x: The writer wants "to say a word in boredom's favour", calling it "the waiting room of imagination". Giving up phones is rejected: "None of this means we should ... throw away our phones".

q: Where do many people say their best thoughts come to them?
o: While playing games on a phone
In a crowded waiting room
In the shower or while on a long walk
While reading their messages
x: The second paragraph says "their best thoughts arrive in the shower or on a long walk". Games and messages are what fill the quiet moments, which the writer sees as the problem.

q: Which advice would the writer most likely give a student looking for fresh ideas for an essay?
o: Spend some quiet time away from screens and let the mind wander
Watch as many videos on the subject as possible
Give up using a phone for a whole year
Avoid walks so as not to waste study time
x: The writer says a wandering mind "occasionally stumbles on an idea" and that a screen may fill "the very space in which original thought begins". A whole year without a phone goes far beyond the five minutes suggested.

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "fruitful" most nearly means:
o: productive
full of fruit
pleasantly sweet
very long
x: A long empty day can be "grim rather than fruitful", that is, unpleasant rather than producing good results such as ideas. "Full of fruit" is the literal meaning, which does not fit a day.

q: In the third paragraph, the writer's attitude is best described as:
o: careful, limiting the claim so as not to overstate it
angry at people who use their phones
doubtful that boredom has any value
enthusiastic about long, empty days
x: The writer admits an empty day "can be grim" and distraction "can be a kindness", then says "My point is narrower". Enthusiasm for long empty days is the opposite of this caution.

q: The passage mainly argues that:
o: film tickets should never be bought in advance
money already spent and lost should not decide what we do next
people should give up any project that runs into difficulty
companies are better than families at managing money
x: Economists warn that a sunk cost "should play no part in decisions about the future", and the writer asks "is the next rupee worth spending?" Giving up at any difficulty is rejected in the last paragraph.

q: Why, according to the passage, does a company keep putting money into a failing project?
o: Stopping would mean admitting that its earlier spending was a mistake
A new project would cost it more over a year
Economists have advised it to keep going
The project is close to success
x: The company carries on "because abandoning it would mean admitting that the earlier spending was a mistake". The cost "over a year" belongs to the family's car, not the company.

q: Which of these decisions would the writer consider sensible?
o: A shopper keeps using a faulty phone because she paid a lot for it
A family keeps repairing an old car because of what they have already spent
A man finishes a dull book only because he bought it
A student leaves a paid course when he sees its remaining classes will not help him
x: The student judges the course "by what lies ahead", as the writer advises; the other three act on money already spent, the very "trap" described. Leaving is not giving up "at the first difficulty", since he has judged the rest useless.

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "abandoning" most nearly means:
o: starting again
hiding
selling
giving up
x: The company keeps paying because stopping the project would mean admitting a mistake, so "abandoning" it means giving it up. Starting again is close to the opposite.

q: The writer's attitude towards people who fall into the trap described is best described as:
o: understanding, though still convinced they are mistaken
scornful, mocking them as foolish
approving, admiring their persistence
indifferent, giving no view about them
x: The writer says "The trap is understandable" but that past spending is "a reason for regret, not a reason to continue". The writer never mocks them, only notes that "no one likes to look foolish".

q: Which sentence best sums up the main point of the passage?
o: Putting things off is mainly a way of escaping unpleasant feelings, and small steps can help
Students who make strict timetables never put off their work
Lazy students rarely finish their essays on time
Tidying one's room is a good way to prepare for study
x: The passage says delay is "less a problem of managing time than of managing feelings" and suggests shrinking "the first step". It rejects laziness: "Hamza is not lazy".

q: What, according to the writer, is wrong with the usual advice to make a stricter timetable?
o: It takes too long to prepare
It leaves no time for rest
It works only for history essays
It says when to start but does nothing about the dread
x: The third paragraph says "A timetable tells us when to start but does nothing about the dread." Nothing is said about the time it takes or about rest.

q: The advice to be kind to oneself after a slip suggests that:
o: delaying does no harm as long as the work is finished in the end
guilt about delaying is itself an unpleasant feeling that can lead to more delay
people who forgive themselves never put things off
timetables work only for people who forgive themselves
x: If delay is a way of escaping unpleasant feelings, then guilt after a slip adds another such feeling, and forgiving oneself removes it; this is why forgivers are "less likely to delay again". "Never put things off" goes too far.

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "stubborn" most nearly means:
o: refusing to obey others
very harmful
rarely noticed
hard to get rid of
x: Because "The relief is immediate; the cost arrives later", the habit keeps returning, so stubborn means hard to get rid of. Refusing to obey describes a stubborn person, not a habit.

q: The writer's attitude towards Hamza is best described as:
o: critical, blaming him for laziness
admiring, praising his tidy room
amused, mocking his poor first sentence
sympathetic, treating his delay as a common human problem
x: The writer defends him ("Hamza is not lazy") and explains his delay through feelings everyone shares. Saying "It was not a good sentence" is followed by "But it was a start", which is kind, not mocking.

q: The writer mainly argues that:
o: parents should teach one language well before any other
growing up with more than one language helps children rather than harming them
children learn their first words mainly from their grandparents
bilingual children are always cleverer than other children
x: The writer calls the parents' worry "largely misplaced" and ends "It is a gift." "Always cleverer" is denied: a second language is not "a magic key to cleverness".

q: What does the writer say a bilingual child must constantly do?
o: Translate her textbooks into her home language
Speak only one language while at school
Avoid using two languages in one sentence
Choose which language to use with each person
x: The third paragraph says she "must constantly choose which language to use with whom". Mixing two languages in one sentence is something such children "do sometimes", not something they avoid.

q: Suppose a father stops speaking Punjabi at home so that his daughter can focus on English. The writer would most likely tell him that:
o: she could keep both languages without harm and might even gain from them
he is right to remove the second language from the home
she will never learn English well while she hears Punjabi
she will become cleverer than all her classmates
x: The writer sees the worry about confusion as "largely misplaced" and lists "quiet advantages" of managing two languages. "Cleverer than all her classmates" goes beyond the passage, which denies a "magic key to cleverness".

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "misplaced" most nearly means:
o: mistaken
lost
hidden
strongly felt
x: The worry is "natural, but ... largely misplaced": the writer goes on to show the mixing is "not signs of confusion", so the worry is mistaken. "Lost", as in a misplaced key, is the everyday meaning, not the one here.

q: The tone of the last paragraph is best described as:
o: anxious and doubtful
boastful and exaggerated
warmly reassuring, while admitting some limits
cold and neutral
x: The writer concedes a second language is not "a magic key" and a child "still needs rich, patient conversation", then calls a home of languages "a gift". The admitted limits rule out "boastful and exaggerated".

q: The passage is mainly an argument for:
o: arranging discussions so that both quick speakers and quiet thinkers are heard
choosing quiet people rather than talkative ones as leaders
doing class projects alone instead of in groups
asking talkative people to stay silent in meetings
x: The writer proposes "a simple change" so that a group "hears from everyone it has gathered". Silencing talkers is rejected: "The point is not to silence the talkers."

q: What does the writer suggest a group should do before anyone speaks?
o: Let the most confident member speak first
Have everyone write down their ideas privately for a few minutes
Vote on which idea is best
Split into a group of talkers and a group of thinkers
x: The third paragraph says "everyone writes down their ideas privately for five minutes before anyone speaks". Letting the confident speak first is the present pattern the writer wants to change.

q: The passage suggests that a group made up only of people who think out loud would most likely:
o: reach better decisions than a mixed group
never argue with one another
miss some mistakes that quieter thinkers would have caught
take longer than any other group to decide
x: "Each catches mistakes that the other misses", so a group with only one style would miss the mistakes the other style catches. Better decisions than a mixed group goes against "Neither style is superior".

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "sharpens" most nearly means:
o: gives them a pointed edge
makes them angry
makes their thinking clearer and quicker
tires them out
x: Out-loud thinkers "need to hear an idea spoken before they can judge it", so argument improves their thinking. Giving something a pointed edge is the literal meaning, used for knives.

q: The writer's view of the two ways of working is best described as:
o: strongly in favour of quiet thinkers
dismissive of people who think out loud
even-handed, seeing value in both
unsure whether either has any value
x: The writer says "Neither style is superior; each catches mistakes that the other misses." Wanting quiet thinkers heard is about fairness, not preferring them: "The point is not to silence the talkers."

q: What does the passage mainly set out to explain?
o: why radio stations should play fewer repetitive songs
what kind of music is played at weddings
how composers write songs that become popular
which tunes tend to get stuck in the mind and a possible reason why
x: It lists the features of "The tunes that stick" and then gives "a clue to why earworms happen at all". Radio and weddings are only places where a tune might be heard.

q: Which feature of tunes that stick is mentioned in the passage?
o: A slow and complicated melody
Very loud instruments
Words in an unfamiliar language
A simple, predictable pattern with one small surprise
x: The second paragraph describes a melody "the ear can predict, yet with one small surprise". The tunes are "usually simple", so a complicated melody is the opposite.

q: If the explanation in the third paragraph is right, which of these would be least likely to get stuck in the mind?
o: A simple chorus heard many times on the radio
A long, complex piece heard once all the way to its end
A catchy tune with one unexpected note
A few lines of a song that stop in the middle
x: Tunes that stick are simple, repeated and unfinished; a complex piece heard once and "to the end" has none of these features, and finishing a song makes the loop "more likely to stop". A fragment that stops in the middle is exactly what the passage says sticks.

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "resolving" most nearly means:
o: making a firm decision
growing louder
being played again
coming to a settled, finished close
x: The fragment is one of "a few lines that stop without resolving", later called "unfinished", "like a question without an answer". Making a firm decision is the commoner meaning, used of people.

q: At the start of the third paragraph, the words "That last feature" refer to:
o: the fact that it is often an unfinished fragment that sticks
the repetition of a chorus many times
the unexpected note in a simple tune
the clear rhythm of the melody
x: The last feature named in the second paragraph is that "a fragment rather than a whole song" sticks, "a few lines that stop without resolving"; the third paragraph then discusses the unfinished. The surprise note was mentioned earlier.

q: The main subject of the passage is:
o: food waste at large weddings and some practical ways of reducing it
why weddings should stop serving meals to guests
how careless and selfish hosts have become
how caterers cook for very large events
x: The passage describes the waste and then the volunteers and smaller portions that tackle it, ending that a wedding "simply needs a plan". Blaming hosts is rejected: "It is easy to blame hosts, but"

q: Why does the writer call "untouched" the key word?
o: Volunteers will not take any food that caterers have cooked
Shelters accept only food that has been frozen
Only food that has not reached a guest's plate can safely be passed on
Untouched food can be sold back to the caterers
x: "Food that has sat on a guest's plate cannot be passed on", so the work depends on the surplus being set aside "before it is served". Volunteers in fact collect food from caterers.

q: Following the reasoning of the second paragraph, which of these would most likely help change the custom?
o: Many families in a community agreeing together to order more modest amounts
One family ordering exactly enough food to set an example
Caterers raising the price of every dish
Guests being urged to eat larger meals
x: The custom is kept alive by the fear of shame, and "No single family can change the custom alone", so a shared agreement would remove the shame of ordering less. One family acting alone is exactly what the writer says will not work.

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "surplus" most nearly means:
o: food that has gone bad
the finest dishes of the meal
the extra food beyond what is needed
money left over after paying the caterers
x: The "surplus" is the food left over when hosts "order far more than can be eaten", set aside "before it is served". The passage speaks of food here, not money.

q: The writer's attitude towards the hosts is best described as:
o: contemptuous of their wastefulness
full of praise for their generosity
indifferent to their difficulties
understanding, seeing them as trapped by a custom
x: The writer says hosts "are caught in a custom that punishes moderation" and explains the "shame of running out". Contempt is ruled out by "It is easy to blame hosts, but".

q: The story told in the passage is mainly about:
o: how losing at chess taught the narrator a habit of thinking before acting
