how the narrator became the strongest player in the club
why Danish was a better player than the narrator
how school chess clubs are organised
x: The narrator "never became very good" but took away "the habit of stopping, before I act, to ask what I am actually hoping will happen". Becoming the strongest player is contradicted.

q: What did Mehwish do after each game?
o: She laughed at the mistakes he had made
She taught him the best opening moves
She refused to play him again
She reset the position where his game had gone wrong and asked him a question
x: She would "set the pieces back to where my position had fallen apart and ask" him what he had hoped for, "without a trace of mockery", so she did not laugh at him.

q: The narrator's feeling that the road was "tilting downhill" suggests that he felt:
o: light and happy, as if things had suddenly become easier
tired after a long and difficult game
nervous about his next game against Danish
worried that he had taken the wrong road home
x: He felt this on the day he first drew against Danish after a month of losing, so walking downhill suggests ease and lightness. Tiredness does not fit the joy of his first good result.

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "trace" most nearly means:
o: a drawing made by copying
a path left behind
the slightest sign
a long delay
x: Mehwish asked "without a trace of mockery", meaning with not the slightest sign of it, which fits her patient help. A drawing made by copying is another meaning of the word, not this one.

q: Looking back on his time in the club, the narrator's attitude is best described as:
o: bitter about having lost so many games
proud of having become a strong player
grateful, valuing what he learned though he never played well
indifferent to the club and its members
x: He says he took something "that I have used far more often than any chess opening", which shows gratitude. He admits "I never became very good", so pride in being strong is wrong.

q: Which statement best sums up the passage?
o: Power cuts in summer make life in a flat unbearable
The narrator's mother was the leader of the building
Mrs Baig had been a famous singer before she moved in
A long power cut unexpectedly brought the neighbours in a building closer
x: Neighbours who barely knew each other spent the night together, and afterwards "Mrs Baig and my mother now drink tea together". "Famous" goes too far: she "had once been a singer".

q: What did Mrs Baig bring to the roof?
o: A plate of sliced mangoes
An old battery torch
A mat to sit on
A jug of water
x: She "arrived with a plate of sliced mangoes". The torch and the water came with the narrator's family, and the mat was the Siddiquis'.

q: It can be inferred that before that night, the families in the building:
o: met on the roof every week
openly disliked one another
often shared meals together
knew one another only slightly
x: The narrator had said "perhaps ... ten words" to Mrs Baig in six years, and the children "had only ever nodded at each other". Nothing suggests dislike, only distance.

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "improbable" most nearly means:
o: impossible to finish
badly told
unlikely to be true
frightening
x: A story about "a buffalo that had followed him home from a market" is hard to believe, so improbable means unlikely to be true. Nothing suggests it frightened anyone.

q: The tone of the final paragraph is best described as:
o: quietly warm, noting a change that lasted
bitter, regretting that the night ended
anxious, fearing another power cut
mocking, making fun of the neighbours
x: Though "the building was itself again", the narrator notes, with warmth, the Sunday tea and the talks on the stairs. There is no regret or fear in the paragraph.

q: What is the passage chiefly about?
o: how the narrator came to own up to a mistake he had tried to hide
how the narrator learned to play cricket more carefully
why Mr Qureshi was angry with the narrator's friends
how the narrator saved up for a new bat
x: After running away, the narrator writes a letter that "simply said what I had done" and delivers it himself. Mr Qureshi "did not look angry", and no bat is bought.

q: Why did the narrator tear up his first two drafts?
o: They were too long for Mr Qureshi to read
They were full of excuses instead of a plain admission
His friends told him not to send them
He had spelt Mr Qureshi's name wrongly
x: The drafts "were full of excuses about the wind and the uneven ground"; the third "simply said what I had done". The passage says nothing about length, friends or spelling.

q: What Mr Qureshi said on the doorstep suggests that he:
o: had chosen to give the narrator the chance to own up himself
had not known who broke the window
had planned to complain to the narrator's parents
was angry that the narrator's friends had not come
x: He "had known it was me all along" yet waited "to see whether I would come", so he deliberately left the step to the boy. Not knowing is contradicted by his own words.

q: As used in the second paragraph, the phrase "wore me down" most nearly means:
o: damaged my clothes
made me angry
made me laugh
slowly tired me and weakened my resistance
x: After days of watching the tired neighbour and waiting, the narrator gave in and wrote the letter, so the silence slowly weakened him. Damaging clothes takes "wore" literally.

q: By calling the experience "the most expensive lesson of my childhood, and the cheapest", the narrator shows that he:
o: regrets having paid for the glass at all
is unsure how much the glass really cost
sees it as costly in money but worth far more than he paid
is still angry that he was made to pay
x: Four months of pocket money was a lot for a boy, yet the lesson was cheap for what it taught. Nothing in the passage suggests regret or anger; he offered to pay himself.

q: The passage is chiefly an explanation of:
o: why leopards are easy to see in a zoo
how hunters track their prey through forests
several ways in which animals avoid being seen
why octopuses are the most skilled of all animals
x: Camouflage "takes several forms", and the passage describes matching, breaking up the outline, countering shadow and changing appearance. The zoo and the octopus are single examples.

q: What, according to the passage, most often gives a hidden animal away?
o: Its colour
Its outline
Its movement
Its smell
x: The last sentence says "Movement, more than colour or shape, is what most often gives a hidden creature away." A hunter is "quick to spot an outline", but movement is named as the commonest giveaway.

q: The passage suggests that a leopard's spots would help it least:
o: on a shady forest floor
on open, evenly lit ground with no shadows
while it is lying completely still
among leaves and branches
x: The spots work by scattering the outline "among the shadows of a forest floor"; where there are no shadows they have nothing to blend with, and they "seem eye-catching in a zoo". The shady forest floor is where they work best.

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "dissolve" most nearly means:
o: mix into a liquid
break into pieces
become sharper
fade from view
x: The spots "scatter its outline" so the edges can no longer be seen clearly; they fade from view. Mixing into a liquid, as sugar does in water, is the commoner meaning.

q: What is the relationship between the second and third paragraphs?
o: It gives more examples of matching the background
It argues against the methods in the second paragraph
It explains how leopards came to have spots
It moves from tricks of colour and outline to a trick that works on light and shadow
x: The second paragraph covers colour and broken outlines; the third begins "A subtler trick deals with light" and explains the pale belly that "cancels the shadow". It adds a method rather than arguing against the earlier ones.

q: What is the central idea of the passage?
o: A small weekly habit, begun with a simple gift, proved more valuable than it first seemed
The narrator's bicycle was stolen and later found by his grandfather
Children should never shake their money boxes
The narrator persuaded his parents to buy him a new bicycle
x: The narrator first thought the pot "a dull present" but later realised "He had given me a habit". He did not ask his parents: "I was too proud to ask".

q: What did the narrator buy with the money from the pot?
o: A brand-new bicycle
A second-hand bicycle and a lock
A present for his grandfather
A new clay pot
x: The pot held "enough for a second-hand bicycle and a lock". The bicycle was second-hand, not new.

q: The stopping of the rattle mattered to the narrator because it:
o: meant that the pot had cracked and had to be broken
told him exactly how much money he had saved
made him decide to break the pot at once
showed that his small coins had added up, which encouraged him to save more
x: The silence meant "the pot was too full for the coins to move"; after that "something shifted" and he began adding notes "every Friday". It could not tell him the exact total, and he broke the pot only years later.

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "fed" most nearly means:
o: gave food to
put money into
emptied out
cleaned
x: He "fed it only when I remembered", meaning he dropped coins into the pot. Giving food is the word's usual meaning, which a clay pot cannot take.

q: In the last paragraph, the narrator's attitude towards his grandfather's gift is best described as:
o: appreciative, seeing its real value
disappointed, still finding it dull
resentful, wishing it had been money
amused, treating it as a joke
x: He realises the gift was "a habit, and the pot was only the excuse", which shows appreciation. Finding it dull was his feeling at eleven, in the second paragraph, not at the end.
